text: Everything in the last lesson's benchmark walk-through — file permissions, service configuration, mounted filesystems — operates on top of the kernel. sysctl reaches a layer below that: it reads and writes kernel parameters live, through the /proc/sys/ virtual filesystem, covering how the networking stack behaves, what the kernel exposes to unprivileged processes, and what happens on disk when a program crashes.

sysctl -a lists every parameter the running kernel exposes — there are hundreds — and sysctl followed by a name reads one, like net.ipv4.ip_forward. A change made with sysctl -w takes effect immediately, but only until the next reboot, which is exactly why real hardening work has to land in a config file rather than stop at a terminal command.

Four settings worth knowing by name: ip_forward, off unless the box is a router, so it can't be repurposed to pivot traffic; suid_dumpable, off so a crashed setuid program can't dump credentials sitting in memory to a readable file; tcp_syncookies, on to defend against a SYN flood exhausting the connection table; and kptr_restrict, hiding kernel memory addresses that certain exploit techniques rely on to defeat kernel ASLR.

The durable version lives in a drop-in file under /etc/sysctl.d/, not a one-off command — the older single /etc/sysctl.conf still works, but drop-in files are the modern convention since they let a configuration tool own one file without touching another team's. Running sysctl --system reads every file there, applies all of them, and the same files get re-applied automatically on every future boot.

Writing the file isn't the same as confirming it worked — a stray space around an equals sign, or a value sysctl silently rejects, can leave the running kernel exactly where it started while the file looks correct at a glance. An engineer re-reads the live parameter after applying it to verify the two actually match. Next up: doing this consistently across a whole fleet of hosts, instead of one server at a time by hand.
